name: Place value & ordering
description: Place value, ordering decimals and negative numbers.

questions.prompt: Tick every number that is greater than 0.5.
questions.explanation: Compare the tenths first. 0.55 is five tenths and five hundredths, and 0.505 is five tenths and five thousandths, so both are greater than 0.5. 0.45 is only four tenths, so it is smaller however many digits follow. The zero in 0.405 is a placeholder in the hundredths column. Reading 0.49 as 'forty-nine' makes it look larger than five tenths, but the 4 is in the tenths column.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is the largest?
questions.explanation: Compare the tenths first: 0.5 has five tenths and the others have four, four and zero, so 0.5 is largest. Counting digits instead of comparing place value makes 0.405 look biggest because it is longest. Reading 0.049 as 'forty-nine' makes it look big, but the 4 is in the hundredths column and there are no tenths at all.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is equal to 3.5?
questions.explanation: 3.50 is 3.5 with a zero after the last digit, which changes nothing. In 3.05 the zero is in the tenths column, so there are no tenths — it is not 3.5. In 0.35 the 3 is in the tenths column, not the ones. 35 is ten times 3.5.

questions.prompt: Tick every number that is less than −3.
questions.explanation: On a number line, further left is smaller. −7, −4 and −3.5 are all left of −3. −2 and −2.5 are to the right of −3, so they are greater: a larger numeral after the minus sign makes the number smaller, not larger.

questions.prompt: Tick every number in which the digit 7 has the value 7 hundredths.
questions.explanation: The columns after the point are tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. In 0.07 the 7 is in the hundredths column, and in 12.074 the 0 holds the tenths column so the 7 is again hundredths. In 0.7 the 7 is tenths, in 7.02 it is units, and in 0.007 it is thousandths.

Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 moves every digit that many columns to the left; dividing moves them right. 0.4 × 100 moves the 4 two columns, giving 40, and 4 × 10 = 40. 0.4 × 1000 moves it three columns, giving 400. 4 × 100 is 400. 40 ÷ 10 moves the digits right, giving 4.

questions.prompt: How many numbers are there strictly between 0.4 and 0.5?
questions.explanation: Between any two different decimals there is always another one: 0.45 sits between them, but so do 0.41, 0.401 and 0.4001, and you can keep going for ever. Counting only the tenths or only the hundredths makes it look as though there is nothing, or only one.

questions.prompt: Write 0.6, 0.06, 0.66 and 0.606 in order, smallest first. Which order is correct?
questions.explanation: Line the numbers up by place value: 0.060, 0.600, 0.606, 0.660. Comparing tenths first gives 0.06 smallest and both 0.6 and 0.606 with six tenths; 0.606 has the extra six thousandths, so 0.66 (six tenths and six hundredths) is largest. Putting 0.6 first counts digits instead of comparing place value. Putting 0.606 last reads it as 606 against 66.

questions.prompt: Tick every number that is less than −2.05.
questions.explanation: −2.5 and −2.2 are both left of −2.05 on the number line, so both are less. −2.005 and −2.0 are to the right: −2.005 is only five thousandths below −2, while −2.05 is fifty thousandths below it. Treating the digit strings 2005 and 205 as whole numbers makes −2.005 look the smaller.

questions.prompt: In the number 12.074, what is the value of the digit 7?
questions.explanation: After the decimal point the columns are tenths, hundredths, thousandths. There is a 0 in the tenths column, so the 7 occupies the hundredths column and is worth 7 hundredths. Calling it 7 tenths skips the zero; calling it 7 thousandths moves it one column too far right; 70 hundredths would be seven tenths.

questions.prompt: Ben works out 0.4 × 100 and writes the answer 0.400. What has he done?

options.text: Added two zeros to the number instead of moving the digits
Rounded the answer to three decimal places

questions.explanation: Multiplying by 100 moves each digit two columns to the left, so 0.4 × 100 = 40. Ben has kept the digits where they are and written extra zeros, which leaves the value unchanged. Multiplying by 10 would give 4, not 0.400, and dividing by 100 would give 0.004. The answer has not been rounded, it has been left alone.

questions.prompt: Dan runs 0.5 km on Monday and 0.45 km on Tuesday. On which day did he run further?

options.text: Both days were the same distance

questions.explanation: 0.5 is 0.50, which is five tenths; 0.45 is four tenths and five hundredths. Comparing the tenths first, Monday is further. Comparing the digits 45 and 5 treats a hundredths count against a tenths count. Having more digits does not make a decimal larger — 0.45 is 0.450, still less than 0.5. The two distances are not the same.

questions.prompt: Tick every number in which the digit 7 is worth 700.
questions.explanation: 700 is seven hundreds, so the 7 must be in the hundreds column. It is in 4,782 and in 40,782. In 7,482 the 7 is in the thousands column, worth 7,000, and in 4,872 it is in the tens column, worth 70.

questions.prompt: Tick every statement that is true.
questions.explanation: 0.5 is five tenths and 0.45 is four tenths, so 0.5 is larger regardless of digit count. Every negative number is less than every positive one, so −0.5 < 0.05; and no negative number is greater than zero, so −0.05 > 0 is backwards.
